idiom_name: typed reorder window (Map<Seq, Envelope> with an expected cursor)
implementation_notes: TypeScript runs on the same single-consumer event loop as JavaScript, so ordering is normally guaranteed by construction - await in sequence, async iterators, ordered Readable streams - and the resequencer is the fallback for genuinely scrambled input. What the type system adds is a contract: brand the sequence number, model the gap policy as a discriminated union (release partial, wait for the gap, discard the hole) and type the window as Map<Seq, Envelope>, so that 'keep last', 'reject old' and 'gap skipped' cannot be interchanged silently. The runtime behaviour is still hand-written; in a Node backend, per-key ordering at the broker is the usual alternative.
pitfalls: Type-only brands do not survive JSON: a sequence number parsed from a broker payload is a plain number, so monotonicity must be validated at the boundary instead of trusted from the type.
Typing the window as Map does not stop iteration-order confusion - the cursor, not the Map, defines the release order.

Discriminated unions make the gap policy explicit but do not enforce that one is chosen: a switch over the policy must be exhaustive (assertNever) or the default branch silently defines production behaviour.
